title: US Quietly Pulls Diplomats' Families From Gulf Posts as Houthi Attacks Escalate
excerpt: Saudi Arabia gets a formal ordered departure while Lebanon, the UAE, Qatar and Jordan quietly trim staffing — leaving families who only just returned facing a second uprooting in a year.
body:
• The United States has ordered non-emergency staff and all family members out of Saudi Arabia and is quietly trimming staffing at embassies in Jordan, Lebanon, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar, CNN reported on Friday.
  • Many of the families had only recently returned to their posts after being evacuated during the Iran war earlier this year, and the diplomats' union says some are being told to leave again without confirmed housing or per diem support.
  • The State Department says all direct-hire personnel and their families are receiving per diem allowances plus lodging and school support, and that the Saudi departure responds to escalating Houthi attacks on airports and oil facilities.
  • For the millions of Indian families living and working across the Gulf, the drawdown is a risk signal worth tracking: four US missions are adjusting staffing under restricted operations, and Washington has warned of possible attacks on Saudi airports and severe travel disruption.

The United States is rushing diplomats and their families out of posts across the Middle East for the second time this year, according to CNN, in a drawdown that officials link to escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and the possibility that the regional conflict widens again. The moves have been made with little public announcement, and the families caught in them describe a chaotic repeat of the evacuation they lived through months ago.

A Second Evacuation in a Year

"To say it has been chaotic is an understatement," one US diplomat told CNN, saying the financial support offered so far does not cover the cost of moving an entire family out of the region. Many families had scrambled to leave in the early weeks of the Iran war, found new housing and schools, and only recently been allowed back. Nikki Gamer, spokesperson for the American Foreign Service Association, the diplomats' union, told CNN: "This echoes the chaos families experienced earlier this year. Some had barely settled back in before being told to leave again. They are understandably upset, confused, and angry."

In a statement on Thursday, the association described "bureaucratic ping-pong" and said families outside Saudi Arabia were being directed to leave without confirmed housing assistance or per diem, because their embassies are not formally changing status.

"Families deserve to know how they will pay for a place to live before they board a plane."

— Nikki Gamer, American Foreign Service Association spokesperson, to CNN

Saudi Arabia Is the Only Formal Departure

This week the State Department ordered the departure of non-emergency personnel and all family members from Saudi Arabia, which officials said was done in response to the Houthi escalations. State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott wrote that Iranian-supported Houthis "have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions." Reuters reported the same order on October 21, noting it came as an attack on Dammam's civilian airport killed at least one person and injured eight, and debris from an intercepted drone targeting the Shaybah oil field killed two people.

Beyond Saudi Arabia, CNN reported, the department has been quietly adjusting staffing caps at embassies including Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, the UAE and Lebanon. A State Department official confirmed to CNN that Lebanon, the UAE, Qatar and Jordan "will see temporary changes to staffing levels under restricted operations," while Kuwait and Bahrain have no personnel changes, suggesting they are not over their caps. Unlike the Saudi order, these movements have not been publicly announced.

Washington's Official Line

The department pushed back on the union's account. A State Department official confirmed to CNN on Friday that all US direct-hire personnel and their families "are getting per diem allowances and support for lodging and schools, with per diem allowances consistent with government rates of where they are geographically in the country." The official added: "We are committed to using every tool available to help families navigate this difficult time, including the added expenses and school enrollment," "Under Restricted Operations Status, staffing levels are constantly evaluated and adjusted," the official said.

The Pressure Behind the Move

The departures come as the Iran-backed Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia — hostilities the State Department has repeatedly warned "have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area." They also come as President Donald Trump has suggested he could relaunch strikes against Iran after the midterm elections, and as sources told CNN that Israel has lobbied, so far unsuccessfully, for more immediate action. For Indian readers, the stakes are close to home: the Gulf states named in the drawdown host the largest concentration of Indian workers abroad, and embassy staffing decisions in Washington are an early, visible gauge of how seriously the US rates the risk of a wider war.
